newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Tjiwi Kimia prices 144a.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Tjiwi Kimia prices 144a.

text.p: Indonesia's Tjiwi Kimia priced its US$600 million section 144a which was upped from US$400 million.
The seven-year issue is non-callable, and was launched at 400 basis points over the underlying U.S. treasuries.
The issuer is rated Ba3 by Moody's Investors Service and BB by Standard & Poor's.
While the Tjiwi Kimia deal attracted interest, bankers said they were looking forward to see the reception given to U.S. dollar deals by Indonesian state banks in coming months.
In other news, bankers said Indonesian state banks might liven up the market.
They had their borrowing allocations approved, but were coming to market in the wake of negative reports by Moody's Investors Service about the Indonesian state banking sector.
One banker said the Indonesian state bank borrowings would be interesting, given Moody's report that it was revising its rating outlook for Indonesian state banks' outlook to uncertain from stable.
The change was made pending decisions on planned mergers in the Indonesian state bank sector, Moody's said.

The state banks would also be putting a "toe into the water" in being the first de facto sovereign issues from Indonesia since the Indonesian rupiah came under speculative selling attack and was effectively devalued, bankers said.
The first issues would show the pricing that the market expected post-devaluation.
PT Bank Persero Negaro Indonesia is in the market with an innovative two-branch US$70 million borrowing for its Singapore and Hong Kong branches.
The Singapore tranche of the three-year floating-rate certificate of deposit (FRCD) is US$40 million, and the Hong Kong branch will get US$30 million.
Bankers said the all-in at the top level was just under 50 basis points.

News that Thailand was ready to talk with the International Monetary Fund was a welcome fillip to debt investors, who have seen several Thai bank deals either repriced or pulled entirely in recent weeks.

"I expect Thailand to be on a continuous growth path and to recover trust from the financial markets as it moves towards reaching agreement on such a programme," Japan's finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said.
In principle, should Thailand request help, Japan would consider it seriously, he added.
But despite good news about Thailand, dealers said investors were still skittish about Asian currencies.
"Today was a good example of how nervous people still are," said one dealer in Singapore.
"All the regionals followed the baht up this morning, but then some corporates said 'oh look, cheap dollars and everything came back."
In other news, Bank of America (Asia) is increasing its FRCD to HK$2.0 billion from HK$1.5 billion.
Bankers said initial response to Agricultural Bank of China's US$120 million five-year FRCD was favourable, although it will not be increased.
